results.title: LLMs through Saussurean and Peircean Lenses
results.content: # LLMs through Saussurean and Peircean Lenses | by Myk Eff | Higher Neurons | Medium. There is a certain elegance in picturing the modern Large Language Model (LLM) hunched over countless sentences, sifting through the labyrinth of words, forging meaning solely from the tenuous interplay of differences. This vision resonates with Ferdinand de Saussure’s view that “in the linguistic system, there are only differences without positive terms” (Saussure, 1959, p. Saussure argued that meaning arises from the negative differentials between signifiers, such that each sign is what it is by not being something else. Charles Sanders Peirce — who famously defined a sign as “something which stands to somebody for something in some respect or capacity” (Peirce, 1931–1958, 2.228) — left ample space for this kind of embodied perception and the power of iconicity and indexicality in sign-making. To the extent that LLMs excel at conversation, they verify Saussure’s insight that meaning emerges from the interplay of signs in a formal system.
